description: We are ready to tackle the challenge and build an impactful prototype using Python and real-world spatial/space data. Excited to explore and innovate for NASA Space Apps 2026!
summary:
AstroArchitect is a web-based space mission and orbital mechanics simulator. It is built to help students, educators, and space enthusiasts understand spaceflight engineering. The tool runs directly in any web browser. It uses React, Vite, and a custom JavaScript physics engine. This engine includes gmat.js, which is inspired by NASA’s General Mission Analysis Tool, or GMAT.

With AstroArchitect, users become mission architects. They choose from a set of curated scenarios, adjust trajectory settings, and run real-time simulations. The results show whether the spacecraft achieves its goals or runs into problems, giving users instant visual feedback.

This approach solves a key problem by making aerospace engineering easier to learn and bringing physics concepts to life. Students no longer need to rely solely on textbooks—they can see how orbital mechanics work in real time. Professional tools like GMAT can be hard for students to understand because they require complex setups and long learning curves. AstroArchitect needs no installation and works right away. It lets users learn through trial and error, turning abstract ideas into fun, hands-on experiences.

AstroArchitect helps the next generation of STEM learners explore spaceflight principles and understand how missions are planned. It makes space engineering feel accessible, makes learning more engaging, and brings the future of space exploration within reach.
details:
What It Is & How It Works: AstroArchitect is a browser-based tool that lets users design space missions and simulate orbital mechanics. Users take on the role of a mission architect: they choose from pre-built scenarios, adjust key orbital settings, and run real-time simulations. Behind the scenes, a custom JavaScript engine—made up of physics.js and gmat.js—calculates orbital motion inspired by NASA’s General Mission Analysis Tool (GMAT). The system displays the spacecraft’s path visually and instantly checks whether the mission succeeds or fails, allowing users to test, refine, and improve their mission designs through hands-on experimentation.

Benefits & Intended Impact:

  • Democratizing Aerospace Education: Professional tools like NASA’s GMAT are powerful, yet hard for beginners to learn. AstroArchitect makes orbital mechanics easier to understand by turning complex math into an intuitive visual experience, allowing students to explore how orbits work without needing years of specialized training.
  • Zero-Barrier Accessibility: AstroArchitect runs directly in any web browser with no need to download software or rely on high-end computers. It works smoothly across devices—from school laptops to mobile phones—anytime and anywhere, making it ideal for classrooms, science fairs, and self-study.
  • Intended Impact: By connecting textbook physics to real mission planning, AstroArchitect inspires students in STEM (Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics) and helps learners understand why certain trajectories succeed or fail through trial and error in a safe, engaging environment.

Tools, Coding Languages & Software Used:

  • Frontend & User Interface: React for building interactive interfaces, Vite for development bundling, JavaScript (ES6+) for core logic, and HTML5/CSS3 for structure and styling.
  • Physics Engine: Custom JavaScript modules (physics.js and gmat.js) that handle orbital calculations, modeled after NASA’s GMAT principles and optimized for real-time web performance.
  • Cloud Deployment & Hosting: Netlify hosts the live application, providing instant global access without any local installation.

Creativity & Design Considerations:

  • Creative Approach: Instead of making orbital mechanics feel like a dry math problem, we transformed it into an interactive mission design experience where users feel like true mission architects. Real-time trajectory visuals and instant status feedback ("Mission Accomplished" or "Mission Failed") turn mistakes into valuable learning moments.
    • Usability vs. Scientific Fidelity: We balanced scientific accuracy—incorporating real orbital rules, velocity thresholds, and trajectory logic—with a clean, approachable interface so beginners are never overwhelmed by unnecessary data.
    • Performance & Cross-Device Compatibility: We optimized the physics engine to run smoothly directly inside the browser, ensuring lag-free performance even on standard or older school computers.
    • Scalability: Our modular architecture allows seamless expansion. New missions, celestial bodies (such as the Moon or other planets), context-aware hints, and collaborative challenges can be easily integrated in future updates.
